name: Friendship 7 / MA-6
first: First American to orbit the Earth
dispatch: Friendship 7 is the flight where the United States finally caught its breath. John Glenn was the first American to orbit — three times around the planet, ten months after Gagarin — and for a country that had spent four years watching the Soviets go first, that was enough to make him the most famous man in the nation overnight. The drama came near the end: a faulty sensor suggested his heat shield might be loose, and controllers had him keep his spent retro-pack strapped on through reentry as a long shot to hold it in place. It held. Glenn came home, and the anxiety that had hung over the whole program lifted with him.
description: John Glenn's 3-orbit flight — first American to orbit Earth, 10 months after Gagarin and 4 months after Titov. Orbit: 159 × 265 km, inclination 32.5°. A heat-shield warning indicator in mission control suggested the shield might be loose — the retropack was kept attached through re-entry as a backup, prompting Glenn's famous "fireflies" observation as bits of retropack ablated past the window. Splashdown 1287 km southeast of Cape Canaveral, 4 h 55 min after launch. Glenn returned to space 36 years later on STS-95 (1998) at age 77. Friendship 7 on display at the National Air and Space Museum, Washington DC.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Atlas LV-3B from Cape Canaveral LC-14 1962-02-20 14:47 UTC.

events.label: ORBIT INSERT
events.note: Insertion into 159 × 265 km Earth orbit, inclination 32.5°.

events.label: "FIREFLIES"
events.note: Glenn reports luminous "fireflies" outside the window — bits of retropack ablating during re-entry.

events.label: SPLASHDOWN
events.note: Capsule splashed down 1287 km SE of Cape Canaveral after 3 orbits / 4h 55min. Recovery by USS Noa.
